knowledgePoints.name: What an agent is
knowledgePoints.teach:
An agent is not a model. It is an autonomous version of Claude running both sides of the messaging loop with no human in the middle: it receives a task, picks a tool, and keeps going until it decides the task is done.

The word that does the work there is both. In a chat application a person supplies every user turn. In an agent, your code supplies them — and what it supplies is tool results.

You own the loop and the tools. Claude owns the reasoning.

Nothing about the API changes. It is the same stateless messages.create, called repeatedly, with the array growing each time.

questions.q: Your team is turning a customer-support chatbot into an autonomous agent that can look up orders and issue refunds without a human approving each step. A junior engineer says the only difference is that the agent uses a bigger context window and a more expensive model tier. What is the structural difference that actually defines the shift from chat integration to agent?
options: The agent uses a model with a larger context window, letting it hold more conversation history before summarizing.
The agent streams its responses token by token instead of waiting for the full completion before displaying anything.
The agent's code supplies every following turn as a tool result, so Claude ends up running both sides of the loop.
The agent persists conversation state in a database server-side, rather than requiring the client to resend the full history.
questions.explain: In a chat app a person supplies each user turn; in an agent, the code supplies tool results as those turns, so Claude ends up driving both sides of the loop with no human in the middle. Larger context and streaming are unrelated capabilities that plenty of ordinary chat integrations also have. Server-side state persistence changes where history lives, not who supplies the next turn.

questions.q: Two engineers disagree about who is responsible for retry logic when a tool call fails inside an agent loop. One says Claude should decide when to retry; the other says the calling code should decide. Based on the ownership split that defines an agent, who owns what?
options: You own the loop and the tools — including retry decisions — while Claude owns the reasoning about what to do next.
Claude owns the loop and decides when to retry a failed call, while your code owns only the tool implementations.
Anthropic's infrastructure owns the loop entirely, and your code is responsible only for the tool definitions you supply.
You own the tool implementations only; Claude owns both the loop's control flow and all retry decisions.
questions.explain: The split is loop-and-tools versus reasoning: your code decides things like whether and how to retry, and Claude decides what to do next given the results. Options putting loop ownership on Claude reverse the actual split. The remaining option moves loop ownership to Anthropic's infrastructure, but the loop is code you write and run yourself, calling the same stateless endpoint repeatedly.

knowledgePoints.name: The five steps
knowledgePoints.teach:
1. Send a message to Claude with tools available.
  2. Claude responds with either a final answer or a tool-use request.
  3. Your code executes that tool.
  4. You send the result back as a tool_result block.
  5. Repeat until stop_reason is end_turn.
while True:
    resp = client.messages.create(model=M, max_tokens=1024,
                                  messages=messages, tools=tools)
    if resp.stop_reason != "tool_use":
        break                                   # ← step 5
    messages.append({"role": "assistant", "content": resp.content})
    results = [run(b) for b in resp.content if b.type == "tool_use"]
    messages.append({"role": "user", "content": results})

The loop's continue condition is stop_reason == tool_use. Its exit condition is end_turn.

Everything else in this cluster is a refinement of these five lines.

questions.q: Your agent implementation has an iteration cap of 25 as a safety net, and on a particular run it exits after only 6 iterations without ever hitting that cap. Nothing in your cap logic fired. What actually caused the loop to end?
options: The tools array became empty because every declared tool had already been called once.
The response Claude returned had a stop_reason of end_turn, so the continue condition no longer held.
The response's content array contained a text block, which your code always treats as terminal.
The conversation reached six messages, which is treated as an implicit default exit point.
questions.explain: The loop's actual exit condition is stop_reason == end_turn; the iteration cap is a safety net you add on top, and in this run the natural exit fired first. Tools aren't consumed by use, so an empty tools array isn't a real mechanism. A text block can appear alongside a tool_use block in the same response, so its presence alone doesn't end anything, and there's no message-count default in the protocol.

questions.q: During a code review, a teammate argues that step 2 of the agent loop — where Claude decides which tool to call — is the step doing the actual work of your system, since it's where the 'intelligence' lives. You want to point out which step is where your own code executes. Which step is it?
options: Step 1, where the tool definitions are assembled and sent along with the request.
Step 2, where Claude decides whether to respond with text or a tool-use request.
Step 5, where the loop's stop_reason is checked against end_turn to decide whether to continue.
Step 3, where your code executes the tool Claude requested and produces a result.
questions.explain: Step 3 is the one instance in the five steps where your own code — not Claude — does the work: it runs the requested tool and produces output. Step 2 is where Claude reasons and decides, step 1 is setup, and step 5 is just a condition check on the response you already received.

reviewQuestions.q: A new engineer sketches the agent loop from memory to onboard onto the codebase, but gets the ordering of two steps backwards. Which of these correctly describes the sequence, from sending the first request through to looping again?
options: Send the request with tools available, receive a tool_use response, execute the tool, send back a tool_result, then repeat.
Send the request with tools available, execute a tool speculatively, receive tool_use back, then send end_turn to repeat.
Execute a tool first, then send the request with tools available, followed by tool_result and tool_use, then end.
Send the request with tools available, receive end_turn immediately, execute the tool, then send tool_result and loop.
reviewQuestions.explain: Claude has to request a tool before your code executes it — the sequence is request, tool_use, execute, tool_result, repeat. Executing speculatively before a request, executing before even sending the request, and treating end_turn as an early step you loop past all invert the actual order, where end_turn is the exit condition rather than a stage in the middle.

reviewQuestions.q: Your team is evaluating whether adopting an agent architecture requires provisioning a different API endpoint than the one your existing chat feature already calls, since 'agent' sounds like a fundamentally different kind of request. What's actually true here?
options: Yes — agents call a dedicated /agents endpoint instead of the standard messages endpoint your chat feature uses.
No — it's the same stateless messages.create call, invoked repeatedly, with the message array growing each time.
Yes, but only once more than one tool is defined; a single-tool agent can still use the standard endpoint.
No, but it does require switching to the streaming variant of the endpoint to support the agent loop.
reviewQuestions.explain: Nothing about the API changes — it's the same stateless call, called in a loop, with the array of messages growing on each iteration. There's no separate agents endpoint, no threshold at which one becomes required, and streaming is an optional choice unrelated to whether something is structured as an agent.

knowledgePoints.name: Name, description, input_schema
knowledgePoints.teach:
A tool is a JSON object with three parts:

{
  "name":        "get_weather",
  "description": "Get the current weather for a city. Use when the user asks
                  about conditions, temperature, or whether to bring a coat.
                  Returns temperature in Celsius and a one-word condition.",
  "input_schema": {
    "type": "object",
    "properties": {"city": {"type": "string"}},
    "required": ["city"]
  }
}

input_schema is standard JSON Schema — a general data-validation specification that long predates any of this and is not AI-specific. If you have written an OpenAPI spec, you already know it.

Convention: name a schema function_name_schema so it pairs visibly with the function it describes. And you can hand your function's source to Claude and ask it to generate the schema.

questions.q: You're writing your first tool definition for a get_weather function and want to make sure you include every required field, no more and no less. Your teammate suggests adding an output_schema field to formally describe the return type. Which set of fields actually make up a valid tool definition, and where is the return type documented?
options: name, handler, and output_schema — with the return type formally declared in output_schema.
name, description, and input_schema — with the return type described in prose inside description.
name, input_schema, and output_schema — with the return type validated against output_schema at runtime.
description, input_schema, and tool_choice — with the return type inferred from input_schema's properties.
questions.explain: A tool definition has exactly three parts — name, description, input_schema — and there is no output schema at all; what the tool returns is documented in prose inside description. Options that include output_schema or a handler field describe something outside the actual spec, and tool_choice is a request-level setting, not part of a tool definition.

questions.q: A developer who has previously written OpenAPI specs is about to write input_schema for a new tool and asks whether it's some Anthropic-specific format they need to learn from scratch. What should you tell them about what input_schema actually is?
options: It's standard JSON Schema, the general-purpose data-validation spec that predates this and isn't AI-specific at all.
It's an Anthropic-designed format for describing tool arguments, similar to JSON Schema but with proprietary extensions.
It's a compiled TypeScript type definition that the SDK converts into a runtime validator automatically.
It's OpenAPI, specifically restricted to the subset used for describing request bodies in REST endpoints.
questions.explain: input_schema is plain JSON Schema — a general specification that long predates tool use and has nothing AI-specific about it, so someone who already knows JSON Schema, or OpenAPI, which is built on it, already knows this. It isn't an Anthropic invention, a compiled TypeScript artifact, or a restricted OpenAPI subset.

reviewQuestions.q: You're reviewing a colleague's new tool definition and notice there's no field anywhere describing the shape or content of what the tool will return when called — no output_schema, no returns property. They ask whether this is a mistake. What should you tell them?
options: It's a mistake — every tool definition should include an output_schema field describing the return shape.
It's fine, but the return format should be documented in the input_schema's `returns` property instead.
It's expected — what a tool returns is described in prose inside the description; there's no dedicated field for it.
It's fine, because Claude infers the return shape automatically from the tool's name and its arguments.
reviewQuestions.explain: There genuinely is no dedicated field for this — the description carries it in prose, which is one reason the guidance calls for three or four sentences rather than one. Adding an output_schema or a returns property isn't part of the actual spec, and Claude doesn't infer return shape from the name or arguments; it reads whatever the description says.

knowledgePoints.name: The field Claude actually reads
knowledgePoints.teach:
The description is what Claude reads to decide whether and when to call the tool.

Not the name. Not the schema. The description. Which makes it the single highest-leverage string in an agent, and:

Vague descriptions are the number one cause of agents misfiring or not using available tools.

The symptom is distinctive: nothing errors. The tool works perfectly when called. It just never gets called, or gets called for the wrong requests, and the agent produces a confident answer it invented instead.

Aim for three or four sentences covering:

  • what it does,
  • when to use it — the part most people omit,
  • what it returns.
WeakStrong
“Searches the database.”“Search customer orders by email address. Use when the user asks about a past order, a delivery date, or a refund status. Returns up to 10 orders, newest first, each with an order id, status, and total.”

questions.q: Your search_orders tool works flawlessly whenever it's invoked directly in a test harness, but in production the agent almost never calls it — instead it answers order questions from general knowledge, sometimes incorrectly. Nothing throws an error anywhere in the logs. Where should you look first to diagnose this?
options: The input_schema, in case there's a required field the agent can never plausibly fill in.
The model tier currently in use, since smaller models may not support tool use as reliably.
The temperature setting, in case it's suppressing tool-use responses in favor of text.
The tool's description, since that's what Claude reads to decide when to call it.
questions.explain: A working tool that's never called, with no error anywhere, is the textbook symptom of a vague description — it's named as the number one cause of agents misfiring or skipping available tools. Schema, model tier, and temperature can all affect other things, but none of them explain a tool that works when called directly yet never gets selected.

questions.q: You're writing a description for a new search_customer_orders tool and want to hit every element the guidance says drives correct selection. A colleague suggests documenting who owns the tool and its typical latency instead. Which three elements should the description actually cover?
options: What it does, who owns it, and how long it typically takes to respond.
Its name, its arguments, and the error codes it can return on failure.
What it does, when to use it, and what it returns to the caller.
What it does, what it costs per call, and when it was last updated.
questions.explain: The three elements are what it does, when to use it, and what it returns — and 'when to use it' is specifically called out as the one most descriptions omit. Ownership, latency, cost, and version history might be useful metadata elsewhere, but none of them help Claude decide whether this tool is the right one for the current request.

reviewQuestions.q: A tool that's available to your agent but never gets called is considered one of the harder failure modes to catch in production, compared to a tool call that errors outright. Why is that specifically?
options: Because the API returns a warning in this case, but it's formatted subtly enough that teams routinely miss it.
Because this particular failure mode only ever manifests once the system is under significant production load.
Because the tool_use block does come back from Claude but then gets silently discarded by your dispatch code.
Because nothing errors at all — the agent just answers without the tool, and the answer looks plausible.
reviewQuestions.explain: There's no failure signal anywhere: no error, no warning, no discarded tool_use block — the agent simply produces a plausible answer it invented instead of a grounded one, which is exactly why it's harder to catch than a call that errors. There's no API warning for this, it isn't load-dependent, and the tool_use block never gets generated in the first place, so there's nothing for dispatch code to discard.

reviewQuestions.q: You have both search_orders and lookup_order_by_id tools, and in production Claude frequently calls the wrong one for a given request — sometimes reaching for lookup_order_by_id when the user only gave a name, or search_orders when they gave an exact id. What's the most direct fix?
options: Sharpen both descriptions, especially the 'when to use it' part, so each tool's scope is explicit.
Rename the two tools so that they sort differently in whatever order the tools array happens to list them.
Remove one of the two tools entirely and merge their input schemas into a single combined schema.
Set tool_choice to any on every request, forcing Claude to weigh both tools each time it's called.
reviewQuestions.explain: Selection between tools is driven entirely by their descriptions, so making each tool's applicability explicit — particularly when to use it — is the direct fix for this kind of confusion. Renaming for sort order has no effect on selection, merging schemas loses the distinction that made two tools useful in the first place, and tool_choice: any doesn't help the model choose correctly between two tools it's already considering.

knowledgePoints.name: Four invariants
knowledgePoints.teach:
The reliable sequence, stated precisely:

  1. Send the user's request and the tool definitions.
  2. Receive an assistant response containing text and/or tool_use blocks.
  3. Execute each requested tool.
  4. Send the complete assistant content back, then a user message containing matching tool_result blocks.
  5. Request the final answer.

Four things must hold, and each has a characteristic failure:

InvariantBreak it and…
Preserve the complete assistant content array, not just the visible textthe tool_use block vanishes and the tool_result has nothing to answer
Each tool_result references its matching tool_use idthe request is rejected as malformed
Every tool_use in a turn gets a resultthe request is rejected — no partial answers
The original tool schemas stay on the follow-up requestClaude no longer knows what the tools were

questions.q: After a tool call, your code appends only the assistant's visible text — not the full content array — to the message history, then sends a tool_result in the next user turn. On the follow-up request, Claude's response makes no reference to the tool's output at all. What went wrong?
options: The tool_use block was dropped from history, so the tool_result you sent has no matching request to answer.
Nothing actually went wrong; the visible text is the only part of the response that matters to the conversation.
The original tool schemas were dropped from the tools array before the follow-up request was sent.
The stop_reason flipped to end_turn prematurely, ending the loop before the tool_result could be read.
questions.explain: The invariant is preserving the complete assistant content array, not just the rendered text — the tool_use block is part of the conversation, and without it the tool_result you send has nothing to answer, so Claude can't connect the two. The text-only view might look complete to a human, but the API still needs the tool_use block for context. Tool schemas and stop_reason are unrelated to this particular failure.

questions.q: In a single turn, Claude's response contains three tool_use blocks. Your code executes all three tools successfully but, due to a bug, only appends two tool_result blocks to the next user message before sending it. What happens when you send that request?
options: Claude proceeds normally using only the two results it was actually given, silently ignoring the third one entirely.
The request is rejected — every tool_use in a turn needs a matching tool_result; partial answers aren't allowed.
The third tool_use ends up being automatically retried by the API itself, before any response is returned to you.
The third tool_use gets treated as though it had returned an error result, and Claude reasons around it.
questions.explain: This is one of the four invariants: every tool_use block in a turn must get a tool_result, and there's no such thing as a partial answer — the request gets rejected outright rather than Claude working around the gap. The API doesn't silently drop, auto-retry, or synthesize an error result for the missing one; it simply refuses the malformed request.

knowledgePoints.name: Tool input is untrusted input
knowledgePoints.teach:
The arguments in a tool_use block were produced by a model, from text that may have come from a user. They are not from your code, and they are not vetted.

Treat tool inputs as untrusted data. Validate authorisation, arguments, timeouts, and side effects before execution.

def run_refund(args, ctx):
    order = db.get(args["order_id"])
    if order.customer_id != ctx.customer_id:   # authorisation — not the model's job
        return error("not your order")
    if args["amount_cents"] > order.total_cents:
        return error("amount exceeds order total")
    ...

The schema already checked that order_id is a string and amount_cents is an integer. It has no opinion about whether this user may refund that order — and neither does the model. Authorisation lives in your executor or it lives nowhere.

The prompt-injection case makes this concrete: a document Claude reads can contain instructions, and if reading it can cause a refund, the document can cause a refund.

questions.q: A process_refund tool's system prompt states 'only refund orders belonging to the requesting customer,' and its input_schema requires an order_id string. During a red-team test, a crafted document read by the agent convinces it to call process_refund on an order belonging to a different customer, and schema validation passes because order_id is a well-formed string. Where should the authorisation check have lived to prevent this?
options: In the description, as an explicit instruction the model is expected to follow before calling the tool.
In the input_schema, as an additional required field capturing the requesting customer's identity.
In your executor code, verifying ownership before the refund's side effect is allowed to run.
In the system prompt, stated more forcefully as a standing rule the agent must always obey.
questions.explain: Authorisation has to live in code that runs before the side effect, because that's the only place it can be enforced rather than merely requested — a document read by the agent can compete with and override anything stated only in the system prompt or description. The schema already validated that order_id is a string; it has no way to check whether this particular customer is allowed to touch this particular order, and adding another field only gives the model more untrusted data to fill in, not real enforcement.

questions.q: Your tool's input_schema successfully validates a process_refund call: order_id is a string and amount_cents is an integer, exactly as required. Your teammate says this means the call is now safe to execute. What has schema validation actually established at this point?
options: That the arguments are now safe to act on, since schema validation is a boundary on Claude's output.
That the requesting user has been formally authorised to perform this exact refund action.
That the referenced order_id and the associated customer both exist in your production database.
That the shape and types of the arguments are correct as declared, and nothing beyond that.
questions.explain: Schema validation checks shape and types only — it can confirm order_id is a string and amount_cents is an integer, and nothing beyond that. Whether the values are real, and whether this caller is allowed to act on them, are questions only your executor code can answer, which is exactly the same boundary structured output has: schemas check structure, code checks truth.

reviewQuestions.q: After your code executes a tool and sends back the tool_result, you also drop the tools array from the follow-up request entirely, reasoning that Claude already knows what happened and doesn't need the definitions again. What breaks as a result?
options: Nothing breaks structurally at all, since only the tool_result blocks themselves are required on the follow-up.
Claude no longer has the tool definitions to reason about, since each call is stateless and nothing carries over.
The follow-up request needs a freshly written system prompt describing the tool's results instead of the schemas.
The tool's actual source code needs to be included in the request for Claude to interpret the result correctly.
reviewQuestions.explain: Each call is stateless, so dropping the tool schemas on the follow-up leaves Claude without the definitions it needs to keep reasoning about the tools in play — the schemas have to stay on every request, not just the first one. It's not enough to send only the tool_result blocks, and neither a rewritten system prompt nor the tool's source code substitutes for the actual schema.

knowledgePoints.name: Two changes, no more
knowledgePoints.teach:
Claude reads all the descriptions you provide and picks per turn — sometimes several tools at once, sometimes one after another across turns.

Adding a tool is two edits:

tools.append(get_weather_schema)         # 1. declare it

def dispatch(block):                      # 2. add a case
    if   block.name == "get_weather": return get_weather(**block.input)
    elif block.name == "search_orders": return search_orders(**block.input)
    ...

Declare it, dispatch it. Nothing about the loop changes.

That is the payoff of the loop being generic: it does not know or care how many tools exist. Which also means the thing that scales badly is not your code — it is the quality of your descriptions, since every added tool makes selection harder.

questions.q: Your agent currently has one tool, get_weather, and you're adding four more: search_orders, refund_order, cancel_order, and send_email. A teammate worries this means rewriting the while loop to handle the extra tool_use blocks that might come back. What actually needs to change to support five tools instead of one?
options: The loop itself, since it currently assumes only a single tool_use block can appear per response.
The tools array, to declare each new schema, and the dispatch function, to add a matching case.
The model tier, since a larger model is needed to reliably reason over five separate schemas.
tool_choice, which must be explicitly set to any once more than one tool becomes available to Claude.
questions.explain: Adding a tool is exactly two edits: declare its schema in the tools array, and add a matching case to the dispatch function. The loop is already generic over however many tools exist, so it doesn't need touching, and neither the model tier nor tool_choice has anything to do with the number of tools declared.

questions.q: With five tools now declared, you notice Claude sometimes calls search_orders even though the tools array happened to list refund_order first, and other times it calls tools in a completely different order across otherwise-similar requests. A teammate assumes selection follows array order. What actually determines which tool Claude picks on a given turn?
options: The order the tools happen to appear in within the tools array sent on that request.
Textual similarity between the tool's JSON schema and the wording of the user's message.
Claude reading all the provided descriptions fresh on every turn and choosing based on them.
Whichever tool was most recently called successfully earlier in the same conversation.
questions.explain: Selection happens by Claude reading every tool's description on every turn, which is also why description quality matters more as the toolbox grows — there's more competing for the same decision. Array order, schema-to-wording similarity, and recency of past calls aren't factors the model bases its choice on.

reviewQuestions.q: You're debugging why your agent takes five separate round trips to look up five independent pieces of information, one tool call per turn, when in principle nothing stops it from requesting all five at once. Is issuing multiple tool_use blocks in a single response actually possible for Claude?
options: No — the API only ever allows a single tool_use block per assistant response, by design.
Only for the small set of server-side tools that Anthropic hosts and executes directly.
Yes, though it often spreads calls across separate turns instead of batching them into one.
Only once tool_choice has been explicitly set to any on that particular request, and not by default.
reviewQuestions.explain: Claude can call several tools in one turn, but its default conservatism often has it spread them across turns instead — which is exactly the behavior the batch tool exists to work around. It isn't limited to one block per response, it isn't restricted to server-side tools, and tool_choice: any doesn't gate whether multiple calls are possible in a single turn.

knowledgePoints.name: Hand it functions, not schemas
knowledgePoints.teach:
The TypeScript, Python and Ruby SDKs ship a tool runner that takes your actual functions, generates the JSON schema from their types and docstrings, and runs the whole exchange internally:

const runner = client.beta.messages.toolRunner({
  model, messages, tools: [getWeather, searchOrders],   // real functions
});
const final = await runner.untilDone();                 // settled final message

What disappears from your code:

  • the while loop,
  • the stop_reason switch,
  • hand-written JSON schemas,
  • manual appending to the message array.

The protocol does not go away. It goes somewhere else.

Which is why the invariants are still worth knowing: when a runner-based agent misbehaves, you are debugging a loop you did not write.

questions.q: You migrate an agent from a hand-written while loop to the SDK's toolRunner, passing it your actual functions instead of hand-authored JSON schemas. A teammate asks whether this means Anthropic's servers now execute your tools and enforce authorisation. What does the tool runner actually take over, and what stays your responsibility?
options: It takes over the while loop, the stop_reason switch, and schema generation — your functions and authorisation stay yours.
It takes over execution of the tools themselves, actually running each one on Anthropic's own infrastructure instead of yours.
It takes over tool selection entirely, ranking the available tool descriptions and deciding which one to call on each turn.
It takes over authorisation checks on every tool argument, validating them against your production database before execution.
questions.explain: The tool runner removes four pieces of mechanism — the loop, the stop_reason handling, hand-written schemas, and manual message appending — but your functions still execute wherever your code runs, and nothing about authorisation moves with it. Execution, tool selection, and authorisation checks all remain exactly where they were; only the surrounding scaffolding disappears.

questions.q: You call `const final = await runner.untilDone()` on an SDK tool runner and want to know exactly what gets returned once the call resolves, so you can decide what to do with it downstream. Which of these is correct?
options: A stream emitting every intermediate message from the run, including tool_use and tool_result turns.
The list of tool names that ended up being called during the run, in the exact order they were invoked.
The last tool_result block produced during the exchange, just before Claude's final reasoning pass runs.
The final assistant message, returned once the internal loop has already run to completion and settled.
questions.explain: untilDone() resolves to the settled final assistant message — the runner has already driven the loop to end_turn internally before returning anything to you. It isn't a stream of intermediate turns, a list of tool names, or the raw last tool_result; those are things you'd have to inspect the runner's internal history for, not what the call itself returns.

reviewQuestions.q: You've switched from hand-writing JSON schemas for each tool to using the SDK's tool runner, passing it your real functions directly. A teammate asks where the schemas Claude actually receives now come from, since nobody is writing them by hand anymore. What's the answer?
options: You still have to write them yourself and pass them alongside your functions to the runner.
Claude infers a reasonable schema on its own, based only on the function's name.
They're fetched at runtime from a shared schema registry maintained by your organization.
They're generated automatically from your functions' types and docstrings by the runner.
reviewQuestions.explain: The tool runner generates the schema from your functions' types and docstrings, which is also a good reason to keep those docstrings accurate — they effectively become the description Claude reads. You're no longer hand-writing schemas, there's no model-side inference from a bare function name, and there's no registry involved; it's derived straight from your own code.

knowledgePoints.name: Primitives beat operations
knowledgePoints.teach:
The instinct when an agent fails at a task is to build a tool for that task. Do it a dozen times and you have a dozen narrow tools and an agent that still fails on anything slightly new.

Claude Code's own toolset is the counter-example:

bash   read   write   edit   glob   grep

Not refactor_code. Not install_dependencies. Not run_the_tests. Six primitives that compose, which is how it handles situations nobody designed for: a refactor is grep, then read, then edit, then bash.

Give Claude abstract, combinable tools rather than hyper-specialised ones.

The trade is real. A narrow tool is more reliable at its one job and needs less reasoning to use correctly. What you buy by giving it up is coverage of the long tail — which, for an agent, is most of what it will meet.

questions.q: Over several months you've built twelve narrow tools for your coding agent — refactor_code, install_dependencies, run_the_tests, and so on — one for each task the agent previously failed at. The agent now reliably handles those twelve tasks but still fails whenever it meets a slightly different request nobody anticipated. Which design principle does this pattern violate?
options: Tools should be kept few enough in number to fit comfortably within the context window.
Tools should be abstract and combinable, rather than narrowly specialised to one predicted task.
Tools should run server-side wherever possible, rather than requiring local execution.
Tools should each do exactly one job, with no overlap between any two tool definitions.
questions.explain: Each narrow tool only covers the exact case it was built for, so a dozen of them still leaves the agent unable to handle anything slightly different from what was predicted — which is precisely what happens here. The fix is tools that compose, like primitives, rather than more single-purpose tools. Context-window limits, server-side execution, and single-responsibility design aren't what's being violated; the problem is coverage of the long tail, not tool count or location.

questions.q: You're designing a toolset for a general-purpose coding agent and want to follow the same design philosophy behind Claude Code's own tools, favoring composability over task-specific coverage. Which of these four toolsets best illustrates that philosophy?
options: refactor_code, install_dependencies, and run_tests — one tool for each common engineering task.
search_orders, refund_order, and cancel_order — one tool per customer-service operation.
bash, read, write, edit, glob, and grep — a small set of generic primitives that combine.
summarise, translate, classify, and extract — one tool per common language task.
questions.explain: This is Claude Code's actual toolset, deliberately kept generic — a refactor becomes grep, then read, then edit, then bash, composed on the fly, rather than one purpose-built refactor_code tool. The other three sets are each collections of task-specific operations, exactly the pattern the principle argues against.

reviewQuestions.q: After replacing several narrow, task-specific tools with a small set of general-purpose primitives, you notice the agent handles novel requests much better but occasionally makes a small mistake on a routine task the old narrow tool used to get right every time. What is this trade-off?
options: Reliability on any single predefined job, traded away in exchange for coverage of the long tail of unpredicted cases.
Nothing meaningful — abstract, combinable tools are strictly better than narrow ones in every situation.
The ability to validate the tool's inputs, since abstract tools generally can't enforce a strict input schema.
Compatibility with the SDK's tool runner, which requires narrowly scoped, single-purpose function signatures.
reviewQuestions.explain: A narrow tool built for exactly one job tends to be more reliable at that one job; giving that up is the real cost of abstraction, paid in exchange for handling the long tail of cases nobody predicted. It's a genuine trade-off, not a strict win, and it has nothing to do with input validation or tool-runner compatibility — abstract tools can still have well-defined schemas.

knowledgePoints.name: Before acting, look; after acting, look again
knowledgePoints.teach:
Claude can only perceive its environment through tool results.

That sentence is the whole topic. An agent has no eyes. If the loop does not feed it fresh state, it is reasoning about the state it last saw — which may be the state it assumed its last action produced.

Concretely:

BeforeAfter
read a file before editing it, so the edit targets current contentread it back, or check the write's return
list a directory before deciding whether to create a filelist again to confirm it exists
screenshot before clickingscreenshot after, to confirm the click landed

Skipping this is a common source of agent failure. The agent flies blind, repeating or compounding an action that silently failed — and reports success, because from inside the loop nothing contradicted it.

questions.q: Your file-editing agent reports 'file saved successfully' at the end of a run, but when you check the repository the file was never actually written — the write call had silently failed partway through. The agent's own transcript shows no error and no contradiction anywhere. Which principle, if followed, would have caught this before the run ended?
options: Using abstract, combinable tools, since a narrower save-only tool would have failed more visibly.
Forcing a specific tool_choice on every turn, so the write step could never be skipped.
Lowering the sampling temperature, to make the agent's reported outcomes more deterministic.
Environment inspection — reading the file back or checking the write's result after acting.
questions.explain: Without a look-again step after the write, nothing in the loop ever contradicts the agent's assumption that the write succeeded, so it reports success from inside a loop that never checked. Tool abstraction, forced tool_choice, and temperature are all unrelated to whether the agent verifies outcomes; the fix here is specifically confirming state after acting, not before.

questions.q: A developer argues that a sufficiently capable agent should be able to reason about whether its own previous action succeeded, without needing an explicit verification step, since the model 'knows' what it just did. Why is that reasoning wrong?
options: Claude can only perceive its environment through tool results, with no other channel available to it.
Tool results are delivered asynchronously and can arrive well after the model has moved on to the next step.
The model discards all context from the previous turn the moment a new tool_use block gets generated.
Success or failure of an action only gets reported back to the agent once the entire loop reaches end_turn.
questions.explain: Perception in an agent is entirely mediated by tool results — there's no other channel, so whatever the loop doesn't feed back in, the model simply doesn't know, no matter how capable it is. The model doesn't discard prior context, tool results aren't inherently asynchronous in this sense, and outcomes aren't withheld until end_turn — the actual gap is that nothing forced a verifying tool call to happen at all.

reviewQuestions.q: A code-review comment asks why your agent's edit routine always reads a file immediately before editing it, even when the agent already read that same file a few turns earlier in the conversation. What's the justification for reading it again right before the edit?
options: To warm a local cache ahead of time so the subsequent edit call can execute with noticeably lower latency.
So the edit targets the file's actual current content, not content merely remembered from earlier turns.
Because the edit tool's underlying API requires the full file contents to be passed as an explicit argument.
To confirm the agent is properly authorised to modify that particular file before the edit proceeds.
reviewQuestions.explain: This is the 'before' half of look-act-look: re-reading immediately before editing ensures the edit targets the file's actual current state rather than a stale memory of it from several turns back, since the file could have changed in between. It isn't about cache warming, an API requirement to pass full contents, or an authorisation check — those are different concerns entirely.

knowledgePoints.name: One tool that holds many calls
knowledgePoints.teach:
Claude can call several tools in one turn. It often plays it safe and calls them one at a time, across several turns — and each turn is a full round trip.

The trick is to give it a single tool whose input schema takes an array of sub-invocations:

{
  "name": "batch_tool",
  "description": "Run several independent tool calls at once.",
  "input_schema": {
    "type": "object",
    "properties": {
      "invocations": {
        "type": "array",
        "items": {"type": "object", "properties": {
          "name":  {"type": "string"},
          "input": {"type": "object"}
        }}
      }
    }
  }
}

Your code unpacks the array, executes each sub-call — optionally in parallel — and returns all the results together as one tool_result.

Use it when the calls are known to be independent. Five city lookups become one round trip instead of five.

The precondition matters: if call two depends on call one's result, batching them is wrong regardless of how much latency it would save.

questions.q: You want to give Claude a way to look up weather for five cities in a single round trip instead of five sequential tool calls, since it tends to call independent lookups one at a time across separate turns. You design a batch_tool whose input_schema needs to carry all five requests at once. What should that input_schema actually accept?
options: A list of tool names to enable for that specific turn, letting Claude call any of them once each.
A single tool name paired with a repeat count, applied identically across all five cities.
An array of sub-invocations, each specifying a tool name and its own input, executed together.
A nested conversation object describing a separate sub-agent run for each city lookup.
questions.explain: The batch tool's input_schema takes an array of sub-invocations, each with its own name and input, which your code unpacks and executes — optionally in parallel — returning all results together as one tool_result. The other designs either don't let each sub-call carry distinct arguments or invent machinery, like a nested sub-conversation, that isn't part of the actual pattern.

questions.q: Your agent needs to look up a customer's order, then use that order's shipping address to look up delivery estimates for that specific address. A teammate suggests wrapping both calls in a single batch_tool invocation to save a round trip. Why would that be the wrong move here, regardless of the latency it might save?
options: Because both calls happen to hit the same backend service, which the batch tool can't route to twice.
Because the second call needs the first call's result as input, so the two calls aren't independent.
Because batching is only ever supported once there are more than five sub-invocations involved in total.
Because all the tools being called here run server-side, and batching simply doesn't apply to those.
questions.explain: Batching's whole precondition is that the calls are independent; here the delivery-estimate lookup needs the order's address as input, so the second call can't run until the first has returned. Same-backend routing, a minimum call count, and server-side-only restrictions aren't real constraints on the batch tool — the actual constraint is data dependency between the calls.

reviewQuestions.q: Your agent needs to look up weather for five independent cities and currently does so across five separate round trips, one per turn, even though none of the five lookups depends on any other. What specific problem is the batch tool designed to solve here?
options: Tool results coming back to the agent out of the order in which the calls were originally issued.
Tool schemas collectively consuming too much of the available context window as more tools are added.
Claude's tendency to call independent tools one at a time across separate turns instead of together.
Claude attempting to call too many tools at once in a single turn and hitting a hard request limit.
reviewQuestions.explain: The batch tool exists specifically because Claude tends to call independent tools one per turn even when nothing requires that — giving it a single tool that accepts an array of sub-invocations collapses those N round trips into one. It isn't addressing result ordering, schema context usage, or a limit on simultaneous calls; those aren't the problem it's solving.

knowledgePoints.name: Buffering, and what turning it off costs
knowledgePoints.teach:
By default, when a tool's input JSON streams, the API buffers and validates it — sending only complete top-level key/value pairs at a time.

That produces the delay-then-burst pattern people notice on a large tool input: nothing, nothing, nothing, then a whole field appears at once.

fine_grained = True   # stream chunks as generated; no server-side JSON validation

You gain immediacy. You lose the API's validation safety net.

With it off, your code may observe invalid or partial JSON — Claude might emit a malformed value such as undefined mid-stream — so it must buffer, validate, and recover deliberately rather than parsing each chunk as it lands.

Worth it for a UI that shows arguments filling in live. Not worth it if you were going to wait for the complete input anyway.

questions.q: While streaming a tool call with a large input payload, your UI shows nothing for several seconds and then the entire argument value appears at once, rather than filling in progressively like the surrounding text does. What causes this specific delay-then-burst pattern?
options: By default the API buffers and validates tool input JSON server-side, emitting only complete key/value pairs at a time.
Tool inputs are always generated only after every preceding text block has finished streaming in full.
Rate limiting is applied specifically to streamed tool-use chunks once they exceed a certain payload size.
The network connection between your SDK client and the API is buffering responses at the transport layer.
questions.explain: By default the API validates tool input JSON and only releases complete top-level key/value pairs, which is exactly what produces the nothing-then-burst pattern on a large field. There's no ordering rule tying tool inputs to text blocks finishing first, no special rate limit on tool-use chunks, and this isn't a transport-layer buffering artifact — it's deliberate server-side validation.

questions.q: You enable fine_grained_tool_streaming so your UI can show a large tool argument filling in live, character by character, instead of appearing all at once. Your teammate assumes this is a free improvement with no other change needed to your handling code. What does your code now need to handle that it didn't before?
options: Content blocks arriving out of the order they were generated in, requiring you to reorder them yourself.
Duplicate tool_use ids appearing within a single response, requiring de-duplication before execution.
Responses coming back with no stop_reason value set at all, leaving you to assume a default yourself.
Partial or invalid JSON, since malformed values can appear mid-stream once server-side validation is off.
questions.explain: Turning off buffering also turns off the server-side JSON validation that came with it, so your code now has to buffer, validate, and recover from partial or malformed values itself — that's the trade fine-grained streaming makes: immediacy for safety. Ordering, duplicate ids, and missing stop_reason aren't consequences of this particular setting.

reviewQuestions.q: Your team is deciding whether to turn on fine-grained tool streaming for a UI that shows tool arguments filling in live as they're generated. Before flipping it on, you want to be precise about what you're actually trading away in exchange for that immediacy. What's the trade-off?
options: Lower per-token cost, traded against modestly higher end-to-end latency for the full response.
Better tool selection accuracy, traded against slightly slower replies from the model overall.
Faster overall streaming throughput, traded against support for a smaller number of declared tools.
Faster, more immediate streaming of arguments, traded against losing the API's server-side JSON validation.
reviewQuestions.explain: The actual trade is immediacy for safety: you get argument chunks streamed as they're generated instead of held until complete, but you lose the server-side validation that used to catch partial or malformed JSON before it reached your code — that validation doesn't disappear, it just becomes your responsibility. Cost, tool-selection accuracy, and the number of tools you can declare aren't affected by this setting at all.
